source_text: Πῶς μέντοι καὶ τοῦτο ἔχει τὸ φιλάλληλον ἐν τῇ φύσει, καὶ ὥσπερ ὁρμαθὸς, ἀλλήλων αἱ νυκτερίδες ἔχονται, καὶ μία τῆς μιᾶς ἤρτηνται· ὅπερ ἐφ' ἡμῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων οὐ ῥᾴδιον κατορθωθῆναι Τὸ γὰρ ἀπεσχισμένον καὶ ἰδιάζον τοῦ κοινωνικοῦ καὶ ἡνωμένου τοῖς πολλοῖς προτιμότερον. Πῶς ἐοίκασι τοῖς ὄμμασι τῆς γλαυκὸς οἱ περὶ τὴν ματαίαν σοφίαν ἐσχολακότες. Καὶ γὰρ ἐκείνης ἡ ὄψις, νυκτὸς μὲν ἔρρωται, ἡλίου δὲ λάμψαντος ἀμαυροῦται. Καὶ τούτων μὲν ἡ διάνοια ὀξυτάτη μέν ἐστι πρὸς τὴν τῆς ματαιότητος θεωρίαν, πρὸς δὲ τὴν τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ φωτὸς κατανόησιν ἐξημαύρωται. Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ δέ σοι καὶ πάνυ ῥᾴδιον πανταχόθεν συνάγειν τὸ θαῦμα τοῦ κτίσαντος. Πῶς μὲν ἐπ' ἔργα σε διεγείρει ὁ σύνοικος ὄρνις, ὀξείᾳ τῇ φωνῇ ἐμβοῶν καὶ καταμηνύων πόρρωθεν ἔτι τὸν ἥλιον προσελαύνοντα, ὁδοιπόροις συνδιορθρίζων, γεωργοὺς δὲ ἐξάγων πρὸς ἀμητόν. Πῶς ἄγρυπνον τὸ τῶν χηνῶν γένος, καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν λανθανόντων αἴσθησιν ὀξύτατον, οἵ γέ ποτε καὶ τὴν βασιλίδα πόλιν περισώσαντο, πολεμίους τινὰς ὑπὸ γῆς δι' ὑπονόμων ἀφανῶν ἤδη μέλλοντας τὴν ἄκραν τῆς Ῥώμης καταλαμβάνειν καταμηνύσαντες. Ἐν ποίῳ γένει τῶν ὀρνίθων οὐκ ἴδιόν τι θαῦμα ἡ φύσις δείκνυσι; Τίς ὁ τοῖς γυψὶ προαπαγγέλλων τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν θάνατον, ὅταν κατ' ἀλλήλων ἐπιστρατεύσωσιν; Ἴδοις γὰρ ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὅπλων παρασκευῆς τεκμαιρομένων τὴν ἔκβασιν. Τοῦτο δὲ οὐ μακράν ἐστι λογισμῶν ἀνθρωπίνων. Πῶς σοι τὰς φοβερὰς ἐπιστρατιὰς τῆς ἀκρίδος διηγήσομαι, ἣ ὑφ' ἑνὶ συνθήματι πᾶσα ἀρθεῖσα καὶ στρατοπεδευσαμένη κατὰ τὸ πλάτος τῆς χώρας, οὐ πρότερον ἅπτεται τῶν καρπῶν, πρὶν ἐνδοθῆναι αὐτῇ τὸ θεῖον πρόσταγμα; Πῶς ἡ σελευκὶς ἐφέπεται ἴαμα τῆς πληγῆς, ἀπέραντον ἔχουσα τοῦ ἐσθίειν τὴν δύναμιν, τοῦ φιλανθρώπου Θεοῦ ἀκόρεστον αὐτῆς τὴν φύσιν ἐπ' εὐεργεσίᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατασκευάσαντος; Τίς ὁ τρόπος τῆς μελῳδίας τοῦ τέττιγος; Καὶ πῶς ἐν τῇ μεσημβρίᾳ ἑαυτῶν εἰσιν ᾠδικώτεροι, τῇ ὁλκῇ τοῦ ἀέρος, ἣν ἐν τῇ διαστολῇ ποιοῦνται τοῦ θώρακος, ἐκδιδομένου τοῦ φθόγγου; Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἔοικα πλεῖον ἀπολείπεσθαι τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θαύματος τῶν πτηνῶν, ἢ εἰ τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῶν ἐπειρώμην ἐφικνεῖσθαι τοῦ τάχους. Ὅταν ἴδῃς τὰ ἔντομα λεγόμενα τῶν πτηνῶν, οἷον μελίσσας καὶ σφῆκας (οὕτω γὰρ αὐτὰ προσειρήκασι διὰ τὸ πανταχόθεν ἐντομάς τινας φαίνειν), ἐνθυμοῦ, ὅτι τούτοις ἀναπνοὴ οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐδὲ πνεύμων, ἀλλ' ὅλα δι' ὅλων τρέφεται τῷ ἀέρι. Διόπερ καὶ ἐλαίῳ καταβραχέντα φθείρεται, τῶν πόρων ἀποφραγέντων· ὄξους δὲ εὐθὺς ἐπιβληθέντος πάλιν ἀναβιώσκεται, τῶν διεξόδων ἀνοιγομένων. Οὐδὲν περιττότερον τῆς χρείας, οὔτε μὴν ἐλλεῖπόν τινι τῶν ἀναγκαίων ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ἔκτισε. Πάλιν τὰ φίλυδρα τῶν ζῴων καταμαθὼν, ἑτέραν ἐν αὐτοῖς κατασκευὴν εὑρήσεις· πόδας οὔτε διεσχισμένους, ὡς τοὺς τῆς κορώνης, οὔτε ἀγκύλους, ὡς τοὺς τῶν σαρκοφάγων· ἀλλὰ πλατεῖς καὶ ὑμενώδεις, ἵνα ῥᾳδίως ἐπινήχωνται τῷ ὕδατι, οἱονεὶ κώπαις τισὶ τοῖς τῶν ποδῶν ὑμέσι τὸ ὑγρὸν διωθούμενοι. Ἐὰν δὲ κατα μάθῃς, ὅπως εἰς βάθος ὁ κύκνος καθιεὶς τὸν αὐχένα, κάτωθεν ἑαυτῷ τὴν τροφὴν ἀναφέρει, τότε εὑρήσεις τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ κτίσαντος, ὅτι διὰ τοῦτο μακρότερον τῶν ποδῶν τὸν αὐχένα προσέθηκεν, ἵνα ὥσπερ τινὰ ὁρμιὰν κατάγων, τὴν ἐν τῷ βάθει κεκρυμμένην τροφὴν ἐκπορίζηται.
orientation: Basil is still expounding the fifth day's creation of birds and water creatures, drawing moral and theological lessons from their natural behaviors.
pass_a_gloss: How indeed also this has the mutual-loving in its nature, and just as a string, the bats hold on to one another, and one hangs from another; which thing among us humans is not easy to accomplish. For the detached and private thing is preferred to the communal and united with the many. How those who have spent their time on vain wisdom are like the eyes of the owl. For also of that one the sight is strong at night, but when the sun has shone it is dimmed. And of these the mind is most sharp for the contemplation of vanity, but for the understanding of the true light it has been dimmed. And by day it is also very easy for you to gather from everywhere the wonder of the Creator. How the house-dwelling bird rouses you to works, crying out with a sharp voice and signaling from afar the sun still approaching, sharing the dawn with travelers, and leading farmers out to harvest. How sleepless is the race of geese, and most sharp for the perception of things that escape notice, who once also saved the royal city, signaling enemies who were already about to seize the citadel of Rome from underground through hidden tunnels. In what kind of birds does nature not show some peculiar wonder? Who is the one announcing to vultures the death of humans, whenever they march against one another? For you would see countless flocks of vultures following the armies, inferring the outcome from the preparation of weapons. And this is not far from human reasoning. How shall I describe to you the fearful campaigns of the locust, which, all lifted up under one signal and encamped across the breadth of the country, does not touch the fruits before the divine command is given to it? How the seleucis follows as a remedy of the blow, having an endless power of eating, the loving God having made its nature insatiable for the benefit of humans? What is the manner of the song of the cicada? And how at midday they are more musical, by the drawing of air, which they make in the expansion of the chest, the sound being given forth? But indeed I seem to fall short in speech of the wonder of winged creatures more than if I tried with my feet to reach their speed. When you see the so-called insects of the winged creatures, such as bees and wasps (for thus they have named them because they show certain incisions from all sides), consider that these have no breath, nor lung, but are nourished whole through whole by the air. Therefore also when drenched with oil they are destroyed, the pores having been blocked; but when vinegar is immediately poured on, they revive again, the passages being opened. Nothing more than the need, nor indeed lacking any of the necessary things, did our God create. Again, when you have observed the water-loving animals, you will find another construction in them: feet neither split, like those of the crow, nor hooked, like those of the flesh-eaters; but broad and membrane-like, so that they may easily swim on the water, pushing through the liquid as with certain oars with the membranes of their feet. And if you observe how the swan, letting down its neck into the depth, brings up food for itself from below, then you will find the wisdom of the Creator, that for this reason he added a neck longer than the feet, so that, letting it down like a certain fishing-line, it may procure the food hidden in the depth.

choices.why: Keeps the compound's force of loving one another, matching Basil's contrast with human detachment
Conveys the image of bats clinging in a chain or cluster
Matches Basil's recurring contrast between worldly philosophy and true light
The verb means joining in the dawn activity, not rousing others; the bird shares the early morning with travelers
Basil explains the name from incisions (ἐντομάς), so the rendering preserves the etymological link
The swan's neck is compared to a line let down to procure food from the depth

pass_b_english: Consider too how this mutual-loving trait exists in their nature: bats cling to one another like a string, each hanging from the next—a thing not easy for us human beings to achieve. For what is detached and private is preferred to what is shared and united with the many. How like the eyes of the owl are those who devote themselves to vain wisdom. The owl's sight is strong at night, but when the sun shines it grows dim. So too their mind is sharpest for contemplating vanity, but for perceiving the true light it has been dimmed.

By day it is very easy for you to gather wonder at the Creator from every side. The bird that lives with you rouses you to work, crying out with a sharp voice and announcing from afar that the sun is approaching, rousing travelers at dawn alongside them and leading farmers out to the harvest. How sleepless is the race of geese, and how sharp their perception of things that escape notice—they once even saved the royal city, revealing enemies who were already about to seize the citadel of Rome through hidden tunnels underground.

In what kind of birds does nature not display some wonder of its own? Who announces to vultures the death of human beings, when they march to war against one another? You could see countless flocks of vultures following the armies, inferring the outcome from the preparation of weapons. This is not far from human reasoning.

How shall I describe to you the fearful campaigns of the locust, which rises all at once at a single signal and encamps across the breadth of the land, and does not touch the crops until the divine command has been given to it? How does the seleucis bird follow as a remedy for the plague, possessing an endless power of eating, since the God who loves humankind made its nature insatiable for the benefit of human beings?

What is the manner of the cicada's song? And how are they more musical at midday, by the drawing of air that they make in the expansion of the chest, as the sound is given forth? But I seem to fall further behind in my account of the wonder of winged creatures than if I tried to reach their speed with my feet.

When you see the winged creatures called insects, such as bees and wasps—for they have been named this because they show incisions on every side—consider that these have no breath and no lung, but are nourished entirely through their whole body by the air. Therefore they are destroyed when dipped in oil, since their pores are blocked; but when vinegar is applied at once, they revive again, since the passages are opened. Our God created nothing superfluous to need, nor lacking in any necessity.

Again, when you study the water-loving animals, you will find a different construction in them: feet that are neither split, like those of the crow, nor hooked, like those of flesh-eaters, but broad and membrane-like, so that they may swim easily on the water, pushing through the liquid with the membranes of their feet as with oars. And if you observe how the swan lowers its neck into the deep and brings up its food from below, then you will discover the wisdom of the Creator—that for this reason he gave it a neck longer than its feet, so that, letting it down like a fishing line, it may procure the food hidden in the depth.

problems.quote: For what is detached and private is preferred by most to what is shared and united.
problems.source_quote: Τὸ γὰρ ἀπεσχισμένον καὶ ἰδιάζον τοῦ κοινωνικοῦ καὶ ἡνωμένου τοῖς πολλοῖς προτιμότερον.
problems.why: Source says the detached is more honored than the shared by the many; English reverses the comparison.
problems.fix: For what is detached and private is preferred by most to what is shared and united.
problems.ruling: Greek has 'προτιμότερον' (preferred/more honored) with genitives: detached [is more honored] than shared; English reverses to 'shared and united is preferred'—meaning inverted.

problems.why: συνδιορθρίζων means 'rousing at dawn together with' or 'waking with the dawn,' not 'sharing the dawn'—the bird wakes travelers, doesn't share dawn with them.
problems.fix: rousing travelers at the dawn with them
problems.ruling: συνδιορθρίζων means 'waking/rousing together with' travelers, not 'sharing the dawn'—action is misidentified.

problems.why: ὁρμιὰν means 'anchor-rope' or 'cable,' not 'fishing-line'—this is a nautical term for the anchor line, not a fishing line. The swan lowers its neck like an anchor rope to reach bottom, not like a fishing line. This changes the imagery significantly.
problems.ruling: ὁρμιὰ means 'anchor-rope/cable,' not 'fishing-line'; nautical imagery of lowering to depth is changed.

edits.old: For what is detached and private is preferred by most to what is shared and united.
edits.new: For what is detached and private is preferred to what is shared and united with the many.
rousing travelers at dawn with them

fixed: Corrected the comparison: source says the detached is preferred to the shared and united with the many, not 'by most'.
Corrected συνδιορθρίζων: the bird rouses travelers at dawn with them, not 'shares the dawn'.
Corrected ὁρμιὰν: it means anchor-rope or cable, not fishing-line.

problems.why: προσελαύνοντα means 'approaching' or 'drawing near,' not 'still approaching'—the adverb πόρρωθεν ('from afar') modifies the announcing, not the sun's motion
problems.fix: announcing from afar that the sun is approaching

problems.quote: rousing travelers at dawn with them
problems.why: συνδιορθρίζων means 'rousing at dawn together with' or 'joining travelers at dawn,' not 'with them' as if the travelers are present; the bird rouses alongside/as travelers do
problems.fix: rousing travelers at dawn alongside them

problems.why: σελευκὶς is the locust-eating bird (probably the hoopoe or similar), not 'seleucis bird' as if it's unclear; it's a specific bird known for following locust plagues
διαστολῇ means 'contraction/expansion' but in breathing terminology refers to the drawing in (expansion) and pressing out; here it's the compression that forces air out for sound
καταβραχέντα means 'dipped' or 'immersed,' not merely 'drenched'—the point is submersion blocking all pores, not just coating

problems.quote: nothing beyond what is needed, nor lacking in any necessity
problems.source_quote: οὐδὲν περιττότερον τῆς χρείας, οὔτε μὴν ἐλλεῖπόν τινι τῶν ἀναγκαίων
problems.why: The Greek says 'nothing superfluous to need/use' and 'nothing lacking to any of the necessities'; 'beyond what is needed' weakens περιττότερον ('superfluous/excessive')
problems.fix: nothing superfluous to need, nor lacking in any necessity

problems.quote: How does the seleucis bird follow as a remedy for the plague
problems.source_quote: Πῶς ἡ σελευκίς ἐφέπεται ἴαμα τῆς πληγῆς
problems.why: ἐφέπεται means 'is applied as' or 'is brought upon,' not 'follows'; the bird is applied as a remedy.
problems.fix: How is the seleucis bird applied as a remedy for the plague
problems.ruling: ἐφέπεται means 'follows after/pursues,' not 'is applied'; the bird follows the locust plague to eat them.

problems.quote: than if I tried to match their speed with my feet.
problems.source_quote: ἢ εἰ τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῶν ἐπειρώμην ἐφικνεῖσθαι τοῦ τάχους.
problems.why: ἐφικνεῖσθαι means 'reach/attain,' not 'match'; and τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῶν means 'with their feet,' not 'with my feet.'
problems.fix: than if I tried to reach their speed with their feet.
problems.ruling: τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῶν means 'their feet' (birds'), not 'my feet'; ἐφικνεῖσθαι means 'reach/attain to,' not 'match.'
